options.metric: Share of crashes involving at least one person injured or killed
options.denominator: Crash records with nonmissing injury and death counts
options.reason: The share of crashes with any casualty is a direct, easy-to-interpret comparison of crash severity across time periods.
options.answer: These data cannot establish whether people face greater risk at night without traffic or travel-exposure data, but 28.27% of nighttime crashes involved an injury or death versus 23.21% of daytime crashes, a 5.06-percentage-point difference.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether a recorded crash is more likely to involve a casualty at night, and shows a higher casualty-crash share at night. It is defensible as a crash-severity comparison, but it leaves unanswered whether an individual trip or hour of travel is riskier at night because traffic and travel exposure are not measured.

options.denominator: Crash records with nonmissing injury and death counts
options.reason: Fatal crashes are the most consequential outcome and show whether recorded nighttime crashes are more likely to be fatal.
options.answer: These data cannot establish whether people face greater risk at night without traffic or travel-exposure data, but fatal crashes occurred at 2.90 per 1,000 nighttime crashes versus 1.08 per 1,000 daytime crashes.
options.interpretation: This framing addresses fatality severity conditional on a crash and shows a higher fatal-crash rate among nighttime records. It is a defensible measure of crash outcomes, but it cannot compare fatality risk per trip or per mile without exposure data.

options.metric: People injured or killed per 100 crash records
options.denominator: Crash records with nonmissing injury and death counts
options.reason: Counting casualties per crash captures the number of people harmed, including multiple victims in a single crash.
options.answer: These data cannot establish whether people face greater risk at night without traffic or travel-exposure data, but crashes produced 40.42 injured or killed people per 100 nighttime crashes versus 30.73 per 100 daytime crashes.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether each recorded nighttime crash carries a larger aggregate human toll, and it shows more injured or killed people per 100 crashes at night. It is defensible because a crash can harm multiple people, but it leaves individual travel risk unanswered without a measure of traffic or travel exposure.
